# @tbrandenburg/node-red-temporal-runtime

A Temporal-backed execution engine for Node-RED flows. It boots a real,
unmodified Node-RED runtime headlessly, and uses the `preRoute`/`onComplete`
hook seam (`RED.hooks`) to let a Temporal Workflow drive message delivery
one node at a time, instead of Node-RED's own local routing.

## Architecture: who owns what

- **Node-RED owns:** node lifecycle and the node/config-node registry,
  credentials, context/storage, source connections (Inject timers, `mqtt
  in`, etc.), **route resolution** (which wired destination(s) a `send()`
  actually reaches, including Link nodes and nested subflows), and the
  deploy/redeploy lifecycle (`lib/bootstrap.js`'s `deploy()`).
- **Temporal owns:** durable scheduling of the *downstream* delivery
  sequence once Node-RED has resolved it, Workflow progress/history,
  retries, and worker-restart recovery (`lib/workflows.js`).
- **Capture is the seam** (`lib/capture.js`): it observes the exact
  destination(s) Node-RED's own `preRoute` hook already resolved for a
  `send()`, suppresses that one external hop's local delivery
  (`done(false)`) so Temporal decides when to re-invoke the next node, and
  otherwise gets out of the way - any hop that stays fully **inside**
  Node-RED's own internal implementation (e.g. both hops of a nested
  subflow) is never captured or suppressed and continues to run as normal,
  local Node-RED delivery.

Concretely: each `executeNode` Activity result carries the `destinationId`
Node-RED's `preRoute` hook already resolved (`lib/activities.js`), and the
Workflow enqueues that captured `destinationId` directly (issue #13) - it
does not re-derive routing from the raw wire graph. A minimal
`nodeId -> wires` graph (`lib/wireGraph.js`) still exists as a fallback for
callers that supply `{port, msg}` without a `destinationId`, but Node-RED's
own resolved routing is authoritative.

Two deployable worker **roles** exist (`lib/worker.js`, issue #16), composed
from the same building blocks:

- **`createActivityWorker`** boots the real Node-RED runtime, installs
  `Capture`, owns source ingress, and polls only the Activity Task Queue for
  `executeNode`. This is the only role allowed to boot Node-RED.
- **`createWorkflowWorker`** registers only the deterministic `executeFlow`
  Workflow code and never boots Node-RED or installs `Capture`. It can run
  as a separate, independently scaled process/deployment.
- **`createCombinedWorker`** (alias: `createWorker`) composes both roles in
  one process on one task queue - today's default, and what the quick
  start below uses.

## Prerequisites

- Node.js >= 22.9 (see `engines` in `package.json`).
- A running Temporal server, reachable at `127.0.0.1:7233` by default
  (override with the `TEMPORAL_ADDRESS` env var). Either:
  - the [Temporal CLI](https://docs.temporal.io/cli)'s dev server:
    `temporal server start-dev`, or
  - a real Temporal cluster.
- Dependencies installed at the repo root: `npm install` (this package is
  not a separate npm workspace; it is hoisted into the repo's flat
  `packages/node_modules/` layout and depends on the sibling `@node-red/*`
  packages via normal `require()`).

## Command sequence

All commands below are run from this package's directory,
`packages/node_modules/@tbrandenburg/node-red-temporal-runtime/`.

The canonical demo flow (`demo/flows.json`) uses a **scheduled Inject**
(fires once ~1s after the worker boots, then every 15s) as its source node,
so starting the worker alone drives the whole flow autonomously - no
separate `start` command is needed to see it running end to end.

1. Start (or reuse) a Temporal dev server in one terminal:

   ```bash
   temporal server start-dev
   ```

   This also serves the Temporal Web UI at `http://localhost:8233`.

2. Start a worker against the demo flow, in a second terminal (blocks in
   the foreground; boots the flow's nodes once and keeps them live):

   ```bash
   node bin/node-red-temporal --flow demo/flows.json
   ```

   On success it prints `worker connected, flowVersion=<hash>,
   taskQueue=node-red-temporal` and keeps running. Within a few seconds the
   demo's scheduled Inject fires on its own - Capture (`lib/capture.js`)
   detects there is no pending Activity for it, and automatically starts a
   new `executeFlow` Workflow Execution per firing (autonomous source
   ingress; see "Architecture" below). No further commands are required to
   observe Workflows being created.

3. Watch it happen either via the Temporal CLI:

   ```bash
   temporal workflow list
   ```

   (one `ingress-<timestamp>-<random>` Workflow Execution per Inject
   firing), or via the Web UI at `http://localhost:8233`, which shows each
   Workflow's Activity list and full event history.

4. Stop the worker with `Ctrl+C` (or `kill <pid>`) once you are done; leave
   the Temporal dev server running if other work still needs it.

### Explicit/debug start path

For debugging a specific node in isolation (e.g. driving a flow that has no
autonomous source node, or replaying a fixed input against one node without
waiting for a real trigger), a Workflow Execution can also be started
explicitly via the CLI's `start` subcommand:

```bash
node bin/node-red-temporal start --flow demo/flows.json --start-node n1 --input '{"payload":"hello"}'
```

This prints the generated `workflowId` (e.g.
`node-red-temporal-1700000000000`) and its `runId`, then exits. This is a
debug/test convenience, not the canonical way the demo is intended to run -
autonomous ingress (above) is primary.

### Split Workflow-worker / Activity-worker deployment (issue #16)

The command sequence above runs a single combined process (`--role
combined`, the default). To run the Workflow and Activity roles as two
independently deployable processes instead, start each with its own
`--role`, pointed at the same task queues:

```bash
# terminal A: Workflow-only worker - never boots Node-RED, never installs Capture
node bin/node-red-temporal worker --role workflow \
  --workflow-task-queue node-red-temporal-workflow

# terminal B: Activity-only worker - boots Node-RED, installs Capture, owns source ingress
node bin/node-red-temporal worker --role activity --flow demo/flows.json \
  --activity-task-queue node-red-temporal-workflow
```

(Using the same string for both `--workflow-task-queue` and
`--activity-task-queue` here is what tells `@temporalio/worker` to route
both Workflow Tasks and Activity Tasks to these two separate processes,
instead of the default single shared queue.) `--address`/`--namespace` and
the `TEMPORAL_ADDRESS`/`TEMPORAL_NAMESPACE` env vars work identically for
both roles and for `start`.

## Use an existing Node-RED editor with a Temporal runtime (issue #39)

The command sequences above all treat `node-red-temporal` as the thing you
run instead of Node-RED, pointed at a static `flows.json` file. That is a
development/debug convenience, not how this package is meant to be used
day to day.

The primary, supported way to adopt Temporal-backed execution is to keep
using your **existing, ordinary Node-RED editor** exactly as before, and
have its normal **Deploy** button ship the flow to a separate
`node-red-temporal` execution runner. Two separate roles are involved:

- **Editor instance ("A")** - an ordinary Node-RED install. Same URL, same
  editor, same palette, same Deploy button. Its own local flows stay
  **stopped** and never execute - it is design-time only.
- **Runner ("B")** - a `node-red-temporal` process (this package) started
  with its Admin API exposed and its editor disabled (`--admin-port`, see
  below). It receives A's deployments and executes them for real, through
  the existing Temporal-backed Activity Worker.

```text
Node-RED A (design time)            Node-RED-Temporal B (execution time)
http://localhost:1880       Deploy  http://localhost:1881 (Admin API only)
normal editor + Deploy  ───────────▶  disableEditor:true
flows kept STOPPED locally           Capture + executeNode Activity Worker
                                      └── Temporal
```

### How it works

A small adapter package installed into A's `userDir` wraps A's existing
Node-RED `storageModule` (whatever it already uses - the built-in
filesystem store or a custom one). It changes nothing about how A stores
its own flows/credentials locally; it only ADDS a remote deployment step:

1. A's normal Deploy button calls Node-RED's own Admin API on A, which
   calls `runtime.flows.setFlows()`, which calls the storage module's
   `saveFlows()` - completely standard Node-RED.
2. The adapter's `saveFlows()` first delegates to A's real storage module
   (so A's local, on-disk flow state is saved exactly as it always was).
3. It then reads A's current, real, encrypted credential bundle via the
   delegate's `getCredentials()`.
4. It performs one full (`Node-RED-Deployment-Type: full`) Admin API v2
   `POST /flows` request - `{ flows, credentials }` - straight to B.
5. B's own `runtime.flows.setFlows()` deploys/redeploys exactly like a
   normal local Deploy would, and B generates its own revision (A's
   revision is never forwarded).

If step 4 fails for any reason (B unreachable, rejected, wrong token,
wrong `credentialSecret`, ...), the adapter's `saveFlows()` **rejects**, so
Node-RED's own Deploy request surfaces a normal error in A's editor - there
is no false "Deploy succeeded" when the remote deploy didn't actually
happen. A's local save may already have completed; simply press Deploy
again once B is reachable.

### 1. Start the runner (B)

```bash
node bin/node-red-temporal worker --role activity \
  --flow demo/flows.json \
  --admin-port 1881 --admin-host 0.0.0.0
```

(`--role combined` also accepts `--admin-port` if you want one process to
be both Activity worker and Workflow worker, today's default topology; see
the split-role section above if you want them separate.) This boots a real
Node-RED runtime with `disableEditor: true` - the Admin API's `POST /flows`
route is served, but no editor HTML/static assets are - and installs
Capture/source-ingress exactly as any other Activity-role worker does. The
node **types** used by the deployed flow must already be installed/available
on this runner, the same requirement as any Node-RED instance.

### 2. Install the adapter into the existing editor's userDir (A)

```bash
cd ~/.node-red      # A's existing userDir
npm install @tbrandenburg/node-red-temporal-runtime
```

### 3. Configure A's `settings.js`

```js
// ~/.node-red/settings.js
const { createRemoteDeployStorage } = require("@tbrandenburg/node-red-temporal-runtime/lib/remoteDeployStorage");
const localfilesystem = require("@node-red/runtime/lib/storage/localfilesystem");

module.exports = {
    // ... your existing settings ...

    // Required: A and B must share the SAME credentialSecret so B can
    // decrypt the credential bundle A forwards. Never rely on Node-RED's
    // auto-generated per-instance key here.
    credentialSecret: process.env.NODE_RED_CREDENTIAL_SECRET,

    // Wrap whatever storage module you already use (the built-in
    // localfilesystem store here, or your own custom one) - it remains
    // fully authoritative for A's local flows/credentials/settings.
    storageModule: createRemoteDeployStorage(localfilesystem, {
        target: process.env.NODE_RED_TEMPORAL_TARGET,   // B's base URL
        token: process.env.NODE_RED_TEMPORAL_DEPLOY_TOKEN // optional, forwarded as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`
    }),

    // Keep A design-time only: flows must not also run locally.
    runtimeState: { enabled: true }
};
```

Local development example (`target`):

```bash
export NODE_RED_TEMPORAL_TARGET="http://localhost:1881"
export NODE_RED_CREDENTIAL_SECRET="a-shared-dev-secret"
```

Remote/cloud example:

```bash
export NODE_RED_TEMPORAL_TARGET="https://node-red-runtime.example.com"
export NODE_RED_TEMPORAL_DEPLOY_TOKEN="$(cat /run/secrets/runner-admin-token)"
export NODE_RED_CREDENTIAL_SECRET="$(cat /run/secrets/shared-credential-secret)"
```

### 4. Restart A, then use it exactly as before

Restart the existing Node-RED process so `settings.js` is reloaded. Open
the same editor URL as before (`http://localhost:1880`). Confirm A's own
flows are stopped/design-only (`runtimeState`/`runtimeFlowState`), then
press the normal **Deploy** button. Verify the deployment reached B (its
logs print `activity worker connected` at boot and each redeploy's revision
is visible via `GET http://<B>/flows`), and that execution now shows up in
Temporal (new Workflow Executions on scheduled/triggered nodes).

### Disabling / reverting

Remove or comment out the `storageModule`/`credentialSecret`/`runtimeState`
block from A's `settings.js`, restart A, and it goes back to being a normal,
fully local Node-RED instance. Uninstalling the
`@tbrandenburg/node-red-temporal-runtime` package from A's `userDir` is
optional and has no effect as long as `settings.js` no longer references it.

### What happens when the runner is unreachable

Every Deploy attempt on A performs a live remote call to B. If B is down,
unreachable, or returns a non-2xx response, the adapter's `saveFlows()`
rejects and Node-RED's Deploy request in A's editor shows a real error -
never a false "Deploy succeeded". A's local flow file may already have been
saved; simply retry Deploy once B is reachable again.

## Recovery demo

`demo/flows.recovery-demo.json` is the same shape as `demo/flows.json` with
a `delay` node inserted between the HTTP request and the tagging step,
giving a deliberate window to kill and restart the worker **between**
Activities (not mid-Activity - see Known limitations below) and observe the
Workflow resume from where it left off, without re-running already-completed
Activities. Sequence:

```bash
node bin/node-red-temporal --flow demo/flows.recovery-demo.json &
node bin/node-red-temporal start --flow demo/flows.recovery-demo.json --start-node n1 --input '{"payload":"hello"}'
# while the delay node's window is open, kill the worker, then restart it:
node bin/node-red-temporal --flow demo/flows.recovery-demo.json
```

The Workflow completes once the restarted worker's Activity poll picks the
Workflow back up; the Temporal Web UI's event history shows the gap and
resumption.

## Known limitations

- **At-least-once Activity execution.** If the worker process is killed
  while an `executeNode` Activity is mid-flight against a side-effecting
  node (e.g. an `http request` node that already fired its HTTP call),
  Temporal will re-schedule and re-run that same Activity on restart,
  re-firing the side effect. The recovery demo above only demonstrates
  killing the worker **between** Activities, which is safe; mid-Activity
  kills are a known, unresolved limitation of this early alpha.
- **Hooks are a process-global singleton.** `RED.hooks` is shared across
  the whole runtime process, not scoped per flow - only one `Capture`
  instance should be installed per worker process.
- **`flowVersion` is pinned with no migration path.** Redeploying a flow
  (`lib/bootstrap.js`'s `deploy()`) changes its content hash; any in-flight
  Workflow still referencing the old `flowVersion` fails loudly with a
  non-retryable `FLOW_VERSION_MISMATCH` - there is no automatic migration
  of in-flight executions to a new flow version.
- **Context/config state is worker-local.** Node, flow, and global context
  (`context.get`/`.set`) survive a worker restart only if a persistent
  Node-RED context store (e.g. the built-in `localfilesystem` store) is
  explicitly configured via `settings.contextStorage` (issue #14); the
  in-memory default context store still does not. Either way, Temporal
  itself does not make context durable - it durably replays the *message
  flow*, not arbitrary worker-local state a node may have written to
  context.
- **Unsupported/non-serializable message shapes.** Some `msg` value shapes
  (circular objects, bare functions, live sockets/streams) do not survive
  the Workflow/Activity boundary intact or fail outright - see "Message
  serialization boundary" below for the full, tested breakdown.
- **HTTP In / HTTP Response is out of scope.** A live `req`/`res` object
  (as used by the `http in`/`http response` node pair) is not bridged
  across the Workflow/Activity boundary; see "Message serialization
  boundary" below.
- **Not tuned for production throughput.** No batching, no worker pooling
  guidance, no benchmarking has been done - this is an early alpha proving
  the execution seam, not a production-ready scheduler.

## Compatibility

`COMPATIBILITY.md` (in this package's directory) is a one-time compatibility
smoke matrix answering "can a representative set of normal Node-RED flow
behaviors run unchanged on top of this runtime?" Exact, current results
(do not round these into a different aggregate percentage): **8/8**
node/runtime-mechanism cases, **10/10** flow-pattern cases, and **2/2**
manual/external-gate cases passing, plus **156/156** passing in the full
`@tbrandenburg` unit suite. See `COMPATIBILITY.md` for the full matrix,
per-case evidence, and explicitly-skipped items (e.g. contrib-node
smoke-testing was skipped by design).

## Architecture: module map

- `lib/capture.js` - `Capture`: installs `preRoute`/`onComplete` (plus a
  scoped, per-invocation `node.error` patch) hooks against a live `RED`
  runtime to observe one node's sends/completion, suppressing local
  delivery (`done(false)`) so Temporal decides the next hop. Correlates
  concurrent invocations by a dedicated `AsyncLocalStorage`-carried
  `invocationId`, not by `_msgid` (see the file's docblock for why).
- `lib/bootstrap.js` - boots a single `flows.json` headlessly through the
  real `@node-red/runtime` (no HTTP/editor), computes a canonicalized
  content-hash `flowVersion`, and exposes `deploy()` for a headless
  redeploy without a process restart.
- `lib/wireGraph.js` - pure transform of flow JSON into a minimal
  `nodeId -> wires` graph; used only as a fallback when a caller supplies
  `{port, msg}` without a `destinationId` (Node-RED's own resolved routing,
  captured by `Capture`, is the primary/authoritative source - see
  "Architecture: who owns what" above).
- `lib/activities.js` - `createExecuteNode`: the Temporal Activity that
  delivers one message to one live node via `Capture.around()` and returns
  its `{sends, error?}`, including the `destinationId` Node-RED resolved.
- `lib/workflows.js` - `executeFlow`: the deterministic Temporal Workflow
  that drains a pending queue of captured `destinationId`s wave-by-wave,
  one `executeNode` Activity call per queued item.
- `lib/worker.js` - `createActivityWorker`/`createWorkflowWorker`/
  `createCombinedWorker` (alias `createWorker`): compose bootstrap +
  `Capture` + the Activity + the Workflow into real `@temporalio/worker`
  `Worker`s, either combined or split across the two roles.
- `bin/node-red-temporal` - CLI: `--flow <path>` runs a combined worker;
  `worker --role combined|workflow|activity` runs a specific role;
  `start --flow <path> --start-node <id> --input <json>` starts a Workflow
  Execution via `@temporalio/client`.

## Manual MQTT-broker E2E gate

The M6 external-source ingress mechanism (any autonomous, non-Activity-owned
`node.receive()`/`send()` starts exactly one Workflow Execution) has automated,
CI-run unit coverage, but that coverage never touches MQTT's actual wire
protocol. `demo/mqtt-e2e-manual.md` documents a **manual, human-run, not
CI-automated** procedure that wires a real `mqtt in` node
(`demo/flows.mqtt-e2e.json`) to a real external MQTT broker, publishes one
message with the already-installed `mqtt` npm client, and confirms exactly one
Workflow Execution starts and completes. See that document for the full
procedure, pass/fail criteria, and why this is a manual gate rather than an
automated one (issue #11).

## Message serialization boundary (issue #35)

Every `msg` that crosses a Workflow-input, Activity-input, or Activity-result
boundary is carried by the Temporal JS SDK's own default Data Converter
(`@temporalio/common`'s `defaultPayloadConverter`, currently `@temporalio/*`
`1.24.0` - see the installed version in this package's `package.json`). This
runtime does **not** configure a custom Data Converter and does not normalize
or pre-serialize messages itself; the table below documents the converter's
*actual observed* behavior for representative Node-RED msg value shapes, per
`test/unit/@tbrandenburg/node-red-temporal-runtime/lib/serialization_boundary_spec.js`.

| Value shape | Category | Observed behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| strings / numbers / booleans / `null` | SUPPORTED | Round-trip unchanged. |
| nested plain objects / arrays | SUPPORTED | Round-trip unchanged (JSON semantics). |
| `Buffer` / binary data | SUPPORTED WITH DOCUMENTED REPRESENTATION | Bytes round-trip exactly, but the converter decodes binary payloads to a raw `Uint8Array`, **not** a `Buffer` instance. Code comparing `Buffer.isBuffer(msg.payload)` downstream of a Workflow/Activity boundary must account for this. |
| `Date` | SUPPORTED WITH DOCUMENTED REPRESENTATION | Round-trips as an ISO-8601 string; the result is a `String`, not a `Date` instance. |
| bare `undefined` value | SUPPORTED WITH DOCUMENTED REPRESENTATION | Round-trips as `undefined`. |
| object property set to `undefined` | SUPPORTED WITH DOCUMENTED REPRESENTATION | The property is silently dropped (standard `JSON.stringify` semantics) - it will not exist on the object that arrives at the next boundary. |
| `Error` object | SUPPORTED WITH DOCUMENTED REPRESENTATION | Round-trips as an empty plain object (`{}`) - `message`, `stack`, and `name` are all non-enumerable and are lost. Do not pass a live `Error` instance as `msg.error` across a Workflow/Activity boundary expecting `.message`/`.stack` to survive. |
| function value (bare) | UNSUPPORTED | Conversion throws (nothing left to JSON-encode). |
| function-valued object property | SUPPORTED WITH DOCUMENTED REPRESENTATION | The property is silently dropped, same as `undefined`. |
| circular object structure | UNSUPPORTED | `toPayload()` throws a `ValueError` naming the unconvertible value - this is the same native failure Temporal surfaces as a Workflow start failure or an `ActivityFailure`/`WorkflowExecutionFailed` when a circular value hits a Workflow input or an Activity result. No wrapping was needed: the native error message already identifies the problem clearly enough to diagnose, so no production code changes were made for this issue. |
| live `net.Socket` / stream-like object | UNSUPPORTED (out of the durable message boundary) | Does not throw, but the converter JSON-flattens whatever enumerable internal fields the object currently exposes into an inert plain-object snapshot - not a usable socket/stream on the other side. Live request/response/socket/stream objects (including HTTP In/HTTP Response `req`/`res`) are explicitly outside the normal durable message boundary and are not bridged by this runtime. |

**Failure behavior:** an unsupported value (e.g. a circular object) reaching
a Workflow input or an Activity result fails via the SDK's own native error
path (a `ValueError` at conversion time, surfaced by Temporal as a visible
start/execution failure) - there is no silent corruption and no fallback to
local Node-RED delivery for such a message.

**Scope note:** this table was produced by testing
`@temporalio/common`'s `defaultPayloadConverter` directly (the same
converter every `proxyActivities`/Workflow/Activity call in this runtime
relies on implicitly). A live-Temporal-server end-to-end smoke for the
binary-payload path was **not** added in this pass: a Temporal dev server
happened to be reachable in the sandbox this work was done in, but it was
started independently of this issue and is shared with other in-flight
work, so exercising it here risked interfering with unrelated parallel
work. The direct Data Converter tests above already exercise the exact
mechanism a live-server E2E would depend on (bytes-in/bytes-out through the
same `toPayload`/`fromPayload` pair used by the real Client/Worker), so they
are sufficient to prove and document the boundary per this issue's
acceptance criteria; a live-server smoke remains a reasonable follow-up if
stronger end-to-end proof is desired.
